title: Vietnam Accessible Tour
text: Roll in Asia is bringing accessible travel to Vietnam! Roll in Asia is the 1st travel agency specializing in accessible vacations for travelers with a physical or mental handicap as well as hearing or visual impairs. Wheelchair accessible? Yes. Travel Vietnam: What to see and experience? Vietnam can be split into three regions: the north, the center, and the south. North Vietnam hosts the capital Hanoi , a metropolis halfway between the traditional way of living and modern lifestyle. The old town of Hanoi is great for sightseeing, shopping, and enjoying the Vietnamese lifestyle. What we particularly like in Hanoi are the little secret places away from the tourist traffic! An excursion to Halong is also a must! Cruise on the Halong Bay or explore the dry land in Halong. They both will amaze you with the spectacular landscapes of endless karst mountains. Central Vietnam is home to the traditions. Hoi An is a fantastic place to explore but it is also the most wheelchair friendly town in Vietnam. The old town is a UNESCO-preserved site with pedestrian streets. Depending on the season, it will also be the perfect spot for beach days. Hue is also in central Vietnam and is the former imperial city with a beautiful citadel. Life in South Vietnam is ruled by the great river: the Mekong! Ho Chi Minh City is the official name of the southern economic (and nightlife!) capital but everybody still calls it “ Saigon .” A trip to the Mekong Delta is a must! Vietnam Accessible Travel Accessible attraction visits and sightseeing of the greatest highlights but also local treasures off the beaten path. We provide specific support from trained guides and assistants. A handpicked selection of accessible restaurants and 3 to 5-star hotels. Adapted local transportation to comfortably welcome wheelchairs. Itineraries are highly personalized to match the specific needs and expectations of each traveler. We ask you to be clear about your specific needs to fully assist you during your travels; each traveler is different. Our website provides a comprehensive list of useful information, ideas for itineraries, pictures, etc. Please contact us for a personalized itinerary suggestion. For more information, please visit rollinasia.com or email info@rollinasia-travel.com .

title: Vietnam: What to Expect & Travel Tips
text: I choose to travel to Vietnam on a whim. I wanted to go to Southeast Asia and I had heard Vietnam was cheap. I also have a bad habit of impulse-buying plane tickets. I took my mom knowing she was adventurous as well. We traveled for 10 days, mainly staying in the North. Overall, I was amazed at how kind and generous people were. I’ll try to provide some insight on travel and getting around Vietnam. Visiting Hanoi We started our trip in the crazy city of Hanoi. There were so many people, motorbikes and traffic! We stayed outside the city at the JW Marriott . Now, in the US this may seem like a fairly expensive hotel, but in Vietnam, it was very reasonably priced. There were many other boutique hotels downtown, but we were more comfortable staying here. I travel in a manual wheelchair mostly so it is easy to take in and out of cars. We took taxis to most places around the city. You must have the address of your destination written down. While many people speak English, we found that it was hard to communicate directions verbally. Have a map and circle where you’re going! We didn’t necessarily need an accessible taxi because I could transfer. The cab drivers were very helpful with my chair also. Downtown Hanoi consists of many side streets and small alleys filled with shops and marketplaces. Of course, because people drive motorbikes, they also park them right on the sidewalk. Most sidewalks are not clear. This gave us no other option than to walk in the street. This was pretty terrifying, but if you just go with the flow people will go around you. Tons of people walk in the street. I can’t think of one shop or store that didn’t have at least one step. Being in a manual chair allowed me to pop up on the curb and explore more freely. Again, people were so helpful and of course always willing to bring out items that I might want to buy. We took two side trips that required travel on a bus. They did not have an accessible bus, but only the 15-passenger van. I was able to manage my way into the bus and folded my wheelchair in the back. My favorite trip was to Halong Bay! We took an overnight boat that cruised through the Bay of Limestone Mountains. Our ship was part of the Paradise Cruises fleet. I probably emailed 30 different companies with little luck in finding a boat with anything close to an elevator. I finally said oh well, if I have to I’ll crawl up the stairs. I’m a bit stubborn when I want to do something. The boat we took had 3 floors, with balconies and gorgeous rooms. The staff insisted they carry me up and down every time I requested – so it worked out well. Intercontinental Air Travel: To Hoi An The second city we visited was Hoi An. This was on the coast and further south, so we had to fly. Although I can transfer easily I can’t walk. I always need an aisle chair to get on and off a plane. It was obvious that the local airports were not used to individuals in wheelchairs traveling. They did have a lift to and from the plane, but I had to sit in the back row and transfer by myself. They also didn’t seem to have an aisle chair. They didn’t seem to understand why I could walk short distances. On budget airlines, flight attendants didn’t know hardly any English. We arrived safely and took a taxi to the hotel. I recommend staying downtown Hoi An because it is along a river. Many streets are closed to cars and traffic, making it a nice walking city. Limited accessible entrances, but plenty to see on the streets without always going inside. Vietnam Travel Tips A manual chair is needed for the easiest travel Have a travel buddy Know keywords for your condition or disability (like “I can’t walk”). This will help people realize what kind of help you may need. Be prepared to be stared at. During my time in Vietnam, I saw one person in a wheelchair. I was an odd site for them, but people were very kind and considerate.

title: Bhutan Wheelchair Accessible Travel
text: Bhutan, known for its serene landscapes and rich cultural heritage, is gradually becoming more accessible to wheelchair travelers. While accessibility may vary, several accommodations, attractions, and public facilities are designed to welcome travelers with mobility challenges. This guide will walk you through the accessible attractions, accommodations (including bed types), pathway conditions, and the location of accessible bathrooms to help make your Bhutanese adventure smooth and enjoyable. Top Accessible Attractions in Bhutan 1. Thimphu – The Capital City The capital is a vibrant city with accessible monasteries, shopping areas, and markets. Many areas in Thimphu have paved pathways, especially around major attractions like the Memorial Chorten and Craft Bazaar. Public accessible bathrooms are available near the Memorial Chorten, the National Textile Museum, and some city parks. Top 2 Attractions: Memorial Chorten: Pathways around the stupa are smooth and paved, though the interior is not fully accessible. Craft Bazaar: Pathways are paved and level, with some stalls at wheelchair height for easy browsing. 2. Tashichho Dzong (Thimphu) This beautiful fortress-monastery houses government offices and monastic quarters. Smooth, paved paths lead to the exterior viewing areas. Interior areas may have steps, so some assistance may be needed. Accessible bathrooms are located near the main entrance and around the visitor areas. 3. Punakha Dzong (Punakha) Known as the “Palace of Great Happiness,” Punakha Dzong is famous for its architecture and riverside location. Accessible ramps allow entry into some areas, and paved pathways cover much of the exterior grounds. Accessible restrooms are located near the main entrance and in the courtyard area. 4. Buddha Dordenma (Thimphu) This massive Buddha statue offers panoramic views of Thimphu Valley. Smooth, paved paths lead to the main statue and viewing platform. Accessible restrooms are available near the base of the statue. 5. Paro Taktsang (Tiger’s Nest Monastery) – Partial Experience Known for its dramatic cliffside location, Tiger’s Nest is a must-see. While the trail itself is not wheelchair-friendly due to rugged mountain terrain, accessible parking and viewing points allow travelers to see the monastery from afar. Accessible facilities are located at the base area where the trail begins. 6. Dochula Pass Scenic mountain pass with 108 chortens and views of the Himalayan range. Smooth pathways allow access to many viewing points. Restroom facilities, including accessible stalls, are available near the viewing areas. 7. National Textile Museum (Thimphu) Learn about Bhutan’s textile history with displays of intricate garments and weaving techniques. Wide, smooth pathways throughout the museum. Accessible restrooms are located in the main lobby of the museum. 8. Paro Valley and Paro Town Paro Valley is home to scenic views, traditional architecture, and vibrant town life. Smooth pavements and accessible curb cuts make the town walkable for wheelchair users. Accessible bathrooms are located at key attractions in Paro, including the Paro Dzong viewpoint and some cafes in town. Accessible Accommodations in Bhutan Le Meridien (Thimphu): Le Meridien offers accessible rooms with wide doorways, roll-in showers, grab bars, and lowered amenities. Accessible rooms are equipped with standard king or twin beds, with low bed frames for easy transfer. Smooth, wide pathways connect rooms with the lobby, dining areas, and outdoor areas. Hotel Zhiwa Ling Heritage (Paro): Accessible rooms with large doorways, roll-in showers, and spacious layouts. Standard rooms come with king or twin beds, and accessible bed heights are designed for easy transfer. Outdoor pathways are generally smooth but may be gravel in some places; staff assistance is available. Public restrooms within the hotel are wheelchair-accessible and include grab bars and low sinks. Amankora (Thimphu and Paro): Accessible rooms with wide entryways, grab bars, and wheelchair-friendly layouts. Most accessible rooms have twin or king beds with lower bed heights. Smooth pathways connect lodge areas; Amankora’s design is suitable for easy wheelchair navigation. Equipped with roll-in showers, grab bars, and lowered sinks. Terma Linca Resort & Spa (Thimphu): Accessible rooms with roll-in showers, grab bars, and lowered light switches and amenities. Accessible rooms come with either king or twin beds, designed for convenient transfer. Smooth, paved pathways connect rooms, dining areas, and the spa. Public restrooms near common areas are accessible and include necessary adaptations for wheelchair users. Accessible Transportation Paro International Airport (PBH): Bhutan’s main airport provides limited accessibility services. Arrange for assistance ahead of time, especially with ramp access and transfers. The airport offers accessible restrooms in the main terminal area. Local Transportation: Private Accessible Vehicles: Due to limited public transport options, private accessible vehicles are the best way to explore Bhutan. Tour operators like Bhutan Accessible Tourism provide vehicles with wheelchair access. Major stops, including Dochula Pass, Paro, and Thimphu, have accessible bathroom facilities at visitor centers or designated rest stops. Tours: Since international visitors must book tours with licensed operators, you can arrange a fully accessible experience with agencies like Bhutan Accessible Tourism. They will provide trained guides, transportation, and accessibility-focused planning for accommodations and attractions. Tips for Wheelchair Travelers in Bhutan Request Equipment in Advance: Some accessible equipment (like portable ramps) can be provided by tour operators with prior arrangement. Prepare for Limited Access at Historic Sites: Many of Bhutan’s heritage sites are partially accessible due to historic structures. If mobility assistance is required, the tour operator can arrange for an extra guide. Check for Restroom Facilities Before Arrival: Restroom availability varies by attraction, so planning ahead for bathroom breaks will help ensure a comfortable visit.

title: Zhangjiajie, China Wheelchair Travel Tips
text: Zhangjiajie, known for its breathtaking landscapes that inspired the floating Hallelujah Mountains in the movie Avatar, is one of the most stunning and wheelchair-accessible destinations in China. This guide covers everything from transportation and attractions to accommodations, restaurants, and essential tips to ensure that wheelchair users can fully enjoy the splendor of Zhangjiajie. Attractions Zhangjiajie National Forest Park : The park offers a mix of smooth, paved paths and boardwalks, allowing easy access to most scenic areas. Some paths have gentle inclines, but are manageable for wheelchair users. Accessible restrooms are available throughout the park, particularly at main entrances and near popular viewing platforms. These restrooms include grab bars, wide stalls, and emergency call buttons. Certain viewing areas may have steps or steep slopes, but alternative routes are often available. Tianmen Mountain : A smooth, glass skywalk and well-paved pathways make this mountain accessible. The skywalk offers a thrilling experience with views through the glass floor, and an accessible pathway circles the summit. Accessible toilets are located at the top and bottom of the mountain, as well as along the main paths. Some sections of the mountain, especially off the main paths, may not be fully accessible, but the key attractions are. Tianzi Mountain : Well-maintained paved paths and elevators at key points provide access to the stunning views. The mountain is part of the larger Wulingyuan Scenic Area, which is also accessible. Accessible restrooms are available at key entry points and within the scenic area, equipped with grab bars and spacious stalls. Some older paths and viewing areas may have steps or uneven terrain, but alternative routes are available. Yellow Dragon Cave (Huanglong Cave) : The cave has smooth, well-lit paths with ramps and elevators that make most areas accessible to wheelchair users. Accessible facilities are located at the cave’s entrance and exit, with grab bars and wide stalls. Some areas within the cave may have narrow passages, but the main sections are accessible. Zhangjiajie Grand Canyon : The canyon features a glass bridge that is wheelchair accessible, along with smooth paths and elevators that make it easy to explore the stunning surroundings. Accessible restrooms are available at the entrance, equipped with grab bars and enough space for wheelchair users. Some paths around the canyon might be uneven, but the main attractions are accessible. Baofeng Lake : The area around Baofeng Lake has smooth, paved paths, making it easy to explore the serene surroundings. Boats on the lake are also wheelchair accessible, with ramps and level access. Accessible toilets are available near the boat docks, with wide stalls and grab bars. Boarding the boats might require some assistance, but the area is generally accessible. Public Transportation Buses : Zhangjiajie has made strides in offering low-floor buses equipped with ramps. These buses provide convenient access to major tourist sites. Most buses can accommodate 1-2 wheelchairs, along with space for 3-4 additional passengers. Not all buses are accessible, so it’s advisable to check ahead with your hotel or use accessible taxis if necessary. Cable Cars and Elevators : The city features cable cars with spacious cabins that can easily accommodate wheelchairs. Additionally, the famous Bailong Elevator, the world’s highest outdoor elevator, is fully accessible, offering a breathtaking ride up the cliffside. Cable cars and the Bailong Elevator can accommodate multiple wheelchairs and several passengers at a time. Some older or smaller cable cars may have narrower entrances, but staff are typically available to assist. Accommodations Crowne Plaza Zhangjiajie Wulingyuan : The hotel offers several accessible rooms with wider doorways, roll-in showers, and lowered amenities. Roll-in showers with handheld showerheads and grab bars are standard. Some rooms also offer accessible bathtubs. Accessible rooms generally accommodate 2 adults, with options for an extra bed or crib. The hotel features smooth, level surfaces throughout public areas, with accessible elevators. Accessible restaurants, a pool with ramp access, and spa services are available. Pullman Zhangjiajie : This hotel offers accessible rooms with roll-in showers, grab bars, and spacious layouts. Roll-in showers with grab bars and non-slip floors, along with accessible bathtubs in some rooms. Rooms can accommodate 2 adults, with suites available for larger groups. Smooth, marble flooring throughout the hotel, with accessible entrances and elevators. Accessible dining, fitness center, and a pool with easy access. Zhangjiajie Huatian Hotel : The hotel provides accessible rooms featuring roll-in showers and grab bars, with lowered switches and handles. Roll-in showers with handheld showerheads and grab bars, as well as accessible bathtubs in some rooms. Rooms typically accommodate 2 adults, with the option to add a bed for a child. The hotel offers smooth pathways with accessible elevators and ramps. Includes an accessible restaurant, spa, and fitness center. Restaurants Fenghuangzhai: Located near the entrance of Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, this restaurant offers step-free access and a spacious interior. Accessible restrooms are available, with grab bars and wide doors. Smooth, level floors throughout the restaurant. Features Hunan cuisine, with local delicacies such as spicy fish. Menus are available in both Chinese and English. Zhangjiajie Xiangxi: This restaurant specializes in local Tujia minority cuisine and is wheelchair accessible, with ramps and spacious seating arrangements. Accessible toilets are equipped with grab bars and wide stalls. Smooth pathways lead to the restaurant, and the interior is level and easy to navigate. Traditional Tujia dishes, with menus available in English and Chinese. The staff is attentive to special needs. The Lobby Lounge (Pullman Hotel): Located within the Pullman Hotel, this lounge offers step-free access and a relaxing atmosphere. Accessible restrooms within the hotel feature grab bars and wide stalls. Smooth, level surfaces with spacious seating arrangements. Offers a mix of Western and Chinese snacks and beverages, with English-speaking staff. Tianmen Lou: Situated near Tianmen Mountain, this restaurant offers ramp access and a spacious interior that accommodates wheelchair users. Accessible restrooms are available with grab bars and wide stalls. The restaurant is situated on a smooth, paved area with easy access from nearby attractions. Specializes in Hunan cuisine, with a variety of spicy dishes and vegetarian options. The menu is available in English, and the staff is accommodating. Public Accessible Toilet Tips Tourist Areas: Major attractions like Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, Tianmen Mountain, and the Grand Canyon all have accessible restrooms. These facilities are generally equipped with grab bars, wide stalls, and emergency call buttons. Restaurants: Many larger restaurants, particularly those connected to hotels, offer accessible restrooms. When in doubt, ask the staff for assistance. Shopping Areas: Key shopping centers and markets in Zhangjiajie have accessible toilets, typically located near elevators or customer service desks. Parks and Scenic Areas: Accessible toilets are a standard feature in the main parks and scenic

title: Shanghai, China Wheelchair Travel Guide
text: Shanghai is one of China’s most accessible cities, offering a mix of historical charm and modern infrastructure. The city’s dedication to accessibility makes it an excellent destination for wheelchair travelers. Attractions The Bund : A smooth, wide pathways along the waterfront with tactile paving for visually impaired travelers. Accessible restrooms are located at various points along The Bund, equipped with grab bars, emergency buttons, and enough space for easy wheelchair maneuvering. Some older buildings may have steps, but most have ramps or alternate entrances. Yu Garden : Traditional stone pathways, mostly even, but some areas are cobbled, which can be bumpy. Accessible restrooms are available, with grab bars and raised toilet seats. Some sections have narrow doorways or steps, but ramps are available in key areas. Shanghai Tower : Modern, smooth floors throughout the tower. Fully accessible restrooms with wide doors, grab bars, and emergency alarms. Minimal; all floors and observation decks are accessible via elevators. Nanjing Road : Flat, wide sidewalks with curb cuts at crossings. Accessible restrooms in most large stores and malls along the road. Crowds can be a challenge, especially during peak shopping times. Shanghai Museum : Smooth, accessible floors with ramps at entrances. Accessible restrooms on every floor, equipped with grab bars and other standard accessibility features. Minimal; well-designed for wheelchair users. Jing’an Temple : Mixed pathways with some areas of smooth stone and others with slight inclines. Accessible facilities are available, though they may be in separate buildings. Some areas may have steps, but ramps are provided in key areas. Shanghai Disneyland : Flat, wide walkways throughout the park, designed with accessibility in mind. Multiple accessible restrooms with baby-changing facilities, grab bars, and wide stalls. Some older attractions may not be fully accessible, but newer rides and shows are designed for all guests. Accommodations The Peninsula Shanghai : This luxury hotel offers accessible rooms with wide doors, roll-in showers, and adjustable beds. Roll-in showers with handheld showerheads, grab bars, and non-slip floors. Some rooms have bathtubs with transfer benches. Accessible rooms can typically accommodate up to 2 adults and 1 child, depending on the bed configuration (e.g., king bed or two twin beds). Smooth marble and carpeted floors throughout the hotel. Accessible spa, restaurants, and a pool with a lift. Hyatt on the Bund : Rooms with roll-in showers, wider doorways, and lowered sinks. Roll-in showers, grab bars, and height-adjustable showerheads. Some rooms offer bathtubs with built-in seating. Rooms generally accommodate 2 adults, with some suites offering space for additional guests (e.g., a sofa bed for a child). Smooth, even surfaces in all public areas. Accessible fitness center and dining options with step-free access. Fairmont Peace Hotel : Historic hotel with modern adaptations, including accessible rooms with wide doorways and roll-in showers. Roll-in showers with grab bars and handheld showerheads. Some suites offer accessible bathtubs. Rooms can accommodate 2 adults, with larger suites available for families or groups. Smooth floors with historic tiles in some areas; ramps have been added where necessary. Accessible rooftop terrace and dining options. Some historic areas may have minor steps or narrow doorways, but alternatives are provided. Public Transportation Metro System : Most metro stations are equipped with elevators, ramps, and clear signage for accessible routes. Accessible restrooms are available at most metro stations, featuring wide doors, grab bars, and emergency call buttons. Each metro train can typically accommodate 2-3 wheelchairs per car, with designated spaces near the doors. Some older stations may have narrow elevators or temporary closures, but staff are generally available to assist. Buses and Taxis : Many buses are low-floor with ramps, and there are accessible taxis available that can be booked via apps. Buses can usually accommodate 1-2 wheelchairs at a time, while accessible taxis can accommodate one wheelchair plus 3-4 additional passengers. Boarding may be challenging during peak hours due to crowded conditions. Public Accessible Toilet Tips Shopping Malls : Large malls like IFC Mall, Plaza 66, and Super Brand Mall have multiple accessible restrooms, typically located on every floor near the main elevators. Restaurants : Chain restaurants and larger establishments often have accessible restrooms, but smaller, older venues may not. It’s advisable to check in advance or ask staff for assistance. Parks and Public Spaces : Major parks like Century Park and Zhongshan Park offer accessible restrooms near main entrances and popular attractions. Public restrooms are generally well-maintained. Metro Stations : Accessible toilets are usually located near station exits or within the station’s ticketed area. Look for signs or ask station staff for directions. Tips : Carrying a RADAR key or similar universal key can be helpful, though most accessible toilets in Shanghai do not require one. Additionally, some public restrooms may require payment, so keep small change handy.

title: Krankin’ thru China
text: Krankin’ thru China was established in 2013 by two Americans and their Chinese friend in an effort to enhance physical and mental wellness among people with disabilities in China. Initially focusing on hand-cycling as an avenue for physical wellness and social interaction, Krankin’ thru China is currently planning to expand into other activities including swimming, yoga, dance, scuba diving, and destination travel with a fitness center of our own based in Beijing, China.

title: China Travel Barriers + Possibilities
text: An image of a wheelchair engraved on a stone dated as early as 5000 years ago was found in China yet the treatment of the disabled in China is unsatisfactory, to say the least. Being Chinese and disabled is hard and in many cases life-ending. Government and public employees that are injured in an accident are supported by the state and accident victims may be compensated at best by the owners of the offender according to his or her abilities. If lucky some receive support from family members but when there is none, the severely disabled will either struggle by themselves or end their own lives. If it wasn’t for some adjustments made before the Beijing Olympic Games 2008, a sightseeing tour was completely impossible for people using wheelchairs. However, many accessible adjustments that were made during the Olympics have been removed and the rest of the country remains not wheelchair friendly. An American citizen can go to Beijing without a Visa for 72 hours only on the condition that he provides an exact itinerary and he can stay only in Beijing. If he wishes to go someplace else or to stay more than 72 hours he needs to have a Visa. It takes not only a visa to travel to China in a wheelchair but more importantly motivation and a positive attitude to conquer the obstacles that await. In China, not only are there no wheelchair ramps but the majority of the time entrances to buildings have an elevated wooden beam, which is a traditional design element to block evil spirits. However, it also creates a barricade for people who use wheelchairs. Wheelchair users are not commonly seen about and about, so when traveling to China expect to see many curious onlookers, which are often not discreet. Most restaurants, shops, and tourist sites are not wheelchair accessible so participants must be flexible and courageous to make it work. China Attractions + Activities (Sample Itinerary) The most popular cities to tour are Beijing, Shanghai, Xian, and Guilin as well as places like Yangshuo, Longsheng, Shuzo, and more. Flights commonly enter Hong Kong. Day 1: In Guilin enjoy a magnificent cruise on the “four lakes” of Guilin, watching the traditional shows along the banks combined with the sight of recently built “old style pagodas” and the special bridges along the route. Then take a short walk along the famous pedestrian zheng yang of Guilin introducing the Chinese souvenir market and bargaining traditions. Day 2: About 2 hours away driving is a place called Longsheng to observe spectacular rice terraces while stopping in the Yao village, swaying short rope bridge crossing, and watching a show by Yao women. Day 3: Take a Guilin panoramic city tour. Visiting the Pearls Museum, followed by a visit to the Silk manufacturing factory, take a walk to the banyan tree near Lake Whangcheng and the gate of the old city wall. Driving over a whang-cheng bridge, viewing the rock elephant trunk, and heading to Yangshou. Over here is a unique experience of a trip to the nearby village by rickshaw. Then perhaps dinner in Yangshou, followed by the “Impression” show which combined traditional Chinese mythology with a modern setup. Day 4: Flight to Xian, the capital city of China for hundreds of years before Beijing. Visit the excavations site of the graves of the Han Dynasty. Day 5: Do a short visit to the ancient city wall. This wall is China’s oldest preserved to this day, and there is an excavation site where the famous terra cotta soldiers were found while visiting all three peers. Back in the city, stroll around the Muslim quarter market and practice bargaining skills. Dim Sam dinner and colorful Tang dance performances are a nice way to end the day. Day 6: Flight to Shanghai and viewing of architecture and lighting, including the bridge to the expo and colonial buildings. Have dinner and a tour of the famous pedestrian 119 Street. Day 7: Visit the Municipal Museum. Take a walk during the day at 119 Street and to a Mongolian restaurant meal. Later view the city from the observatory on top of the Jin Mao. From there, go to an acrobatic performance. End by taking a cruise on the river, watching the city from this special angle of view. Day 8: Travel to the Jewish district and visit the museum and the local synagogue. Stroll along the Bund Promenade, looking across the city in the daylight compared with the previous day’s night and an interesting perspective of the TV tower and buildings Expo 2005. Take a short drive to the Old City and stroll through the alleys. Off the street, Nangin 580 is filled with markets. Day 9: Heading towards the city of Suzhou. Here visits a local house of farmers raising crabs having a chance to travel along the road and watch the scenic village and fields. Then visit a classic Chinese garden which is by itself part of Chinese artwork. The local market is adjacent to the garden. Day 10: Taking the bullet train from Shanghai to Beijing. The train travels at about 300 Km/Hr and it takes about 6 hours for the trip. A meal with a glimpse of one of Beijing’s famous markets, the “silk market,” where you can find everything at ridiculous prices. Do not be mistaken, all the products there are fake but it is very tempting! Then to the biggest TV screen in the world and spend the rest of the night at a nearby jazz club. About Wheelchair Sizes, Shapes + Types Maximum wheelchair dimensions are 63cm (width) by 90cm (length), and 7.5cm is the minimum distance from the ground. This is because the door to public transportation does not exceed this. If there is a vehicle anchor bolt it must be dismantled. All other battery charges such as a cell phone or a laptop preferably also 220 volts (each room is also a 110-volt socket with questionable reliability). On occasion, a wheelchair-using participant will need to pee at a remote location where there are no modern toilets. When this happens the tour leader will provide a shelter to enable go to the bathroom into some kind of cup or jar. Power Wheelchairs: Motorized chairs must be able to travel without recharging for at least 4mi. The battery’s connection cable must be easily accessible and have quick connect/disconnect. The electrical voltage is 220 volts (the US is 110v), therefore a participant needs to prepare. The best idea is to get an adapter. At most hotels, you may find a 110 volts socket, adapted to an American plug in the bathroom. This is good for an electrical shaving machine or to charge a cell phone but it is not suited for charging the batteries of a power wheelchair. Manual Wheelchairs: There is a fee for those that use manual wheelchairs and need assistance with pushing. This will be needed in sporadic cases e.g. Tiananmen and the Forbidden City require traveling about 1km. The maximum body weight for participants traveling in a manual wheelchair by himself or herself should not exceed 90 kg. If more than 90 kg then the participant needs to provide his or her escort. Airport Wheelchair Details Gel batteries are the only batteries excepted in China and one must have documentation. Chairs with battery acid/fluid are illegible for flights and will not be uploaded on the plane. Batteries should be disconnected for each flight. Chinese rules and regulations regarding domestic flights allow only one disabled person with an escort on each flight. To bypass this restriction, the additional wheelchair-using passengers will have to sign a responsibility waiver disclaimer. Security checks at airports in China also for the disabled confined to a chair can be very unpleasant. One should overcome this with humor. Flights departing Beijing are famous for the severe test. Luggage at airports is x-rayed. All metal parts, cosmetic preparations, water bottles, magnets, scissors of all sizes, nail files, etc. should fit into checked luggage. Lighters are completely forbidden. Chinese authorities do not compromise on that and “violating objects” are confiscated and discarded. Truckloads of cell phones and laptops, and batteries of different types should disassemble and fit into suitcases. For guests from the States, the best and cheapest way to go to China is to have a flight to Shanghai. There are many direct flights from New York and Los Angeles to Shanghai. Flights to Beijing and or Hong Kong take much longer, are more expensive and there are almost no direct flights to those destinations. China Transportation Transportation may be the biggest obstacle for people in wheelchairs in China. Suitable buses that are equipped with ramps are numerous, owned by the government, and scarcely available for private use. Ramps into buses or private vehicles are very steep so assistance is almost always needed. In Hong Kong, there are only two buses available equipped to serve up to five disabled persons with non-folding wheelchairs. Shanghai has only one such bus. In any case, these buses have limited space inside, not suitable for non-folding wheelchair chairs. In other words, you need to be able to transfer. The Bullet Train is very wheelchair accessible with elevators and a level platform to get onto the train. Sometimes trains are not 100% accessible but you can make it work. Chinese regulations do not require safety belts on the cars and do not have any available–bring your own if needed. Hotels Wheelchair accessible hotel rooms are rare and below many developed countries’ standards. Not every hotel in China is wheelchair accessible. The “problem” is that there are only two rooms for the disabled in each hotel, which is true almost all over China. These rooms are big enough to have two electrical wheelchairs and sometimes will have an additional bed. In most cases, the bed is a double bed (unlike a twin room) and one has to cope with that. The standard rooms at the hotel that we chose have a door that enables a wheelchair to go through but not necessarily to the bathroom. At check-in, it is common for a hotel to ask for your passport and sometimes it is returned the following day Money can be exchanged at hotels but not always returned within 24hs In some places, the room air conditioner is interrupted at night and/or changed to a uniform temperature Damages in the hotel rooms and mutilation of bedding and towels (staining) are chargeable at a hotel rate Breakfasts consist of a rich mix of Western and Chinese items Some hotels will provide a complimentary bottle of water per day but other than that food and beverage items in rooms are charged Laundry services are available at most hotels Food + Beverage Hotels are the most accessible places to get food but this is certainly not always the case. Entering most restaurants is a challenge because of a traditional one-step barrier 15cm high. Authentic food in China is delicious and fresh but is very different from food in America so one needs to have an open pallet. High-quality restaurants will be selected If you tour with OFEK Travel Tour but in most places, travelers will be able to find McDonald’s and KFC, and sometimes Starbucks as well. If a picky eater then perhaps bring items like canned tuna, crackers, and instant noodles from home. Do not eat the food on the streets. The western stomach is usually not strong enough to digest it and with the poor availability of suitable toilets, it might become quite a disturbance. The menu is fixed and there are almost no flexibilities. Some places serve food buffet style with a variety of dishes and some traditional Chinese food like dim-Sum. At most restaurants quantities are smaller and the food is served on a rotating serving platter with eight dishes that people have to coordinate and share. Food includes soups, like corn soup or similar. Sticky white rice is unlimited. Seasoned Chicken and or pork slices are common along with steamed cabbage and some vegetables. Sometimes fish and shrimp are available. Don’t plan on seeing French fries but instead, lots and lots of noodles, found almost everywhere, including at convenience stores in which you prepare it yourself with hot water. Hot water can be found almost anywhere. Soft drinks are available for purchase in restaurants and convenience markets. Do not drink tap water in China! You can get very cheap bottles of water everywhere. Those are not “mineral water” but are drinkable. In most cases, the driver has water bottles that you can buy at a very low price Public Toilets One of the biggest challenges to traveling to China in a wheelchair is the toilets. A few popular places, like the Great Wall, the sacred way, the Forbidden City, and more will have better luck. The Chinese are custom squatting over toilets so toilets with seats are rare. Even at restaurants most of the time seats are not accessible. Do not expect to find accessible restrooms in American chain fast food restaurants, like McDonald’s. There is no way around it, such obstacles make a wheelchair journey to China a challenge indeed, so it is recommended to bring dispensable cups to use in case of emergency.

title: China Vacation Accessibility Tips
text: I would like to share some of my wheelchair experiences while on vacation in China with my wife. First, let me tell you that I am not a writer by any means. I just wanted to capture some of the issues we had to work out while traveling abroad. I will preface this by saying the trip was fantastic and very exciting. I am glad I went and can’t wait to try another country or countries. Planning a Trip to China My wife planned the entire China vacation. She had learned about the particular tour company called China Odyssey Tours.com from a co-worker that had been there a couple of years ago. She contacted the company and asked if it was possible to accommodate a tour for someone in a wheelchair. They asked several questions about what that would entail, and she provided as many answers as she could. We determined together that it was worth a try. The tour company did their best to make traveling work but it was by no means perfect. I had been preparing to travel since I was an inpatient at the Shepherd Center. I went with the therapeutic recreation department to the Atlanta airport to learn how to navigate the airport in a wheelchair and board planes. Once I moved to outpatient, I started going to the peer support group at the Shepherd Center to ask questions about international traveling. I attended the Wheelchair Skills Clinic to help learn how to navigate curbs and rough terrain. I also visited the Shepherd Center Seating Clinic to see what suggestions they had for my chair. I will say all this did help, but I noticed that through all the advice I got that everyone’s experience is going to be a little different. So with all the advice in hand, I packed my bags as efficiently as possible. I brought some extra things that were suggested just in case. I brought an adjustable wrench and an Allen wrench set to be able to make adjustments to my chair if necessary. The seating clinic noticed my front casters were starting to flake from everyday use, so I ordered a couple of extra casters to bring along in case they decided to go bad while I was in China. I made sure I had enough catheters and toiletries to last me in case something went wrong. The one thing that I was sure of was that something was going to go wrong while we were there, and I had talked to my wife about that. We were as prepared as we could be. However, nothing could prepare us for what was going to happen. After all the preparations, it was time to go. I will not lie. I was nervous but also excited to be going on a trip of this magnitude. Although I have been to international destinations before, I felt like this was my first trip anywhere. We flew from Atlanta to Detroit and Detroit to Beijing. I knew I was going to have to use the restroom on the Beijing flight. I had gone over several scenarios to do this. (e.g., Using a foley catheter, using an intermittent catheter at my seat under a blanket, etc.) My wife noticed one of the restrooms was marked with a handicap sign, so I asked the flight attendant if they had an aisle chair. They said they did, so I decided to give that option a shot. While I would not suggest this option to a lot of wheelchair users, it did offer the most privacy. Most notably, the aisle chair did not have a footrest, so I had to hold my legs in the air while they pushed me. I waited until the cabin was dark and everyone was asleep to go. Almost all the flight attendants were on break in the upstairs area of the plane. One flight attendant wheeled me back to the restroom. I was able to get in using the handle on one side of the restroom and the sink on the other and pushing myself to a standing position. Everything was going well. I did my thing and was ready to go. I opened the door and the flight attendant was waiting on me. I was standing at the door when the other flight attendants were ready to come off their break. They tried to open the door to the stairway, but my aisle chair was blocking their door. One of the flight attendants accidentally pulled the smoke alarm in the stairwell while waiting for me. This promptly woke up everyone on the plane and had them looking at me in the door trying to get back in the aisle chair. The captain had called to see what was going on as well. I will say it was a bit embarrassing. After getting back to my seat, my wife just smiled at me. I knew we were both thinking to ourselves that hopefully, this is all that will go wrong. Beijing We arrived in Beijing late in the evening and met our first tour guide. The Beijing airport is very large and busy. This was the site of the first challenge to see what kind of vehicle they would have and how to get into it. It turned out they had a van with a sliding door. I was able to transfer to the floor of the van and pull myself up to the seat. Things went fairly well. We were in a hurry, so I took the chair apart, so we could get it in quickly. The driver was later able to put the two back seats up and they were able to put the chair in the back without taking it apart. The tour group sent this message to all the other cities we were to visit, so they were prepared for us. We got to our hotel at about midnight. Our hotel room at Regent Beijing was perfect. It was wide enough to fit any size chair. The bed was low, and the room had a large roll-in shower with a permanent bench. We slept well that night and were ready for site seeing in the morning. We met our tour guide and driver and were off. We went to Tiananmen Square . It was flat and smooth. We went to the pedestrian crossing that went under the street to go to the Forbidden City. While this was a ramp, it was grooved to provide traction for snow. This is how the majority of the ramps were constructed in Beijing. I was able to use the ramp, but I had to go down backward and do wheelies to get up it. It wasn’t much of a problem. We made it to the entrance to the Forbidden City . The area wasn’t cobblestone, but it wasn’t exactly smooth either. I had to do lots of wheelies to get around. I wasn’t concerned until what happened next. I was taking pictures and was behind my wife and the tour guide. Something felt wrong with my chair, but I kept moving to keep up. The next thing I know the back completely broke off my chair. It broke off at the top bolt holding the back on. I called my wife and the tour guide. We looked at each other and just had a sinking feeling. We had 11 more days in China, and my chair was broken! We stared at each other for what felt like hours but was just a few minutes. The tour guide had no idea what to do. Finally, I said that I needed to get out of the chair and get the back completely off to see what we can do. I transferred to a curb and took the Velcro off and got the backoff. As luck would have it, my tools were in the hotel room. At first, I told her that we needed to go back to the hotel. She called the driver and told him to meet us on a side street about a half-mile away. It was not a comfortable roll in the wheelchair, but I was able to manage it. We met the driver and were going to get in the van, but I noticed all the bicycles around. I asked the tour guide if there was a bike shop or anywhere we could find a drill in this area. She asked several people and someone said there was a guy down an alley on the street that worked on bicycles. We went a few blocks looking down each ally and found the guy working on bicycles. I told her what I needed, she relayed the information to him, and the bicycle guy went to work. He had Allen wrenches, a hacksaw, and a drill with only 1 drill bit. He cut the broken part off the bottom of my chair, drilled 4 new holes, and reattached the back. It was about 4 inches shorter, but it would work to get me through the trip. We were back on track and went to the Forbidden City. In the Forbidden City, there were some ramps to go through the different areas, but I would not say it was wheelchair accessible. Several times I would have to hop onto the ground, throw my chair over a large threshold and then hop back in my chair. Upon leaving the Forbidden City, we were following the crowd down the sidewalk. This posed another challenge. They have lots of bollards to keep bikes off the sidewalks. I had to try several areas until I found one that I could fit through. There were probably 3 sets of them, but I was able to just make it through all 3 without having to get out of my chair. We got back to our vehicle and were off to lunch. The majority of restaurants we ate at had the same issues. There were generally 3 or more steps to get in with no accessible ramps. The wait staff generally had no problem picking me up in my chair to get into and out of the restaurants. The other issue was restrooms . I found that most of the restroom doors were not wide enough for me to get in. In those that were wide enough, there were no handicap stalls. The stalls were also generally up another stair for plumbing. I learned not to be shy and would do my business in a corner urinal. As a side note about China restrooms, my wife had several issues because most restaurants don’t have commodes like we are used to. Most were just holes in the floor. The next day we were off to see the Great Wall . We were told there was one section of the Wall that was handicap accessible, so that is where our guides were taking us. The term handicap accessible is a very loose term in China (even looser than in the US). We went up a windy road and found a parking place in one of the highest lots. You could see the Great Wall from this area, but we were a good distance from it. The driver came with us and proceeded to push me up a steep, roughly tiled street. It was too steep for me to do it on my own. We made it to a landing where we purchased tickets to go to the wall. This entailed a gondola ride up the side of the mountain. My chair wouldn’t fit into the gondola, so I had to transfer into the gondola and quickly take it apart. The gondola operators were not happy that they had to slow the gondola down. We got out at the top and then there were more sets of stairs. The builders had tried to make a ramp, but it was at the same incline as the stairs, roughly 1 to 1. Although it was against my better judgment, the driver pushed me up the ramp to the lookout for the Great Wall. I was not technically able to get on the Great Wall as those stairs were very uneven with no ramp, but I was able to touch it and get a close view of it. Going back down was probably more nerve-racking than going up. I had to go down the ramps and road backward because they were so steep. I kept hearing the driver’s feet slipping. If he fell, I would have been in a lot of trouble. I will say it is possible to do, but it would be nice to have more than 1 person pushing! We were done in Beijing, and we were off to the airport. We thought a lot about the flight from the States to China, but we didn’t think much about the flights inside China as they were arranged by the travel agent. We flew on China Airways. The airports in China were immaculate and fully handicap accessible; however, that is not to say we didn’t have several issues arise on these flights. Xian Our first issue came on our flight from Beijing to Xian. This was a security issue. After my chair broke, I decided to keep my tools with me in case I had any more problems. I have a set of Allen wrenches (no more than 3 inches long and not sharp) and a small adjustable wrench. According to the TSA in the States, this is acceptable to have on your carry-on. The safety personnel in Beijing confiscated them from me. They did give me a chance to check them in my luggage, but our luggage was long gone and our English-speaking guide was gone, so I just let them have it and hoped nothing else would go wrong. Other than that, boarding the plane in Beijing was just like the States. When we arrive in Xian, they did not have an aisle chair to get me from my seat to the tunnel to get in my chair. I put my arms around two flight attendants, and they dragged me to my waiting chair in the jetway. We immediately started our tour in Xian . We went to the wall surrounding the city. It was not accessible at all by a wheelchair, so I waited for my wife to look around. We also visited several pagodas and temples. You can see a lot, but you cannot get into the temples or pagodas, so I wheeled around and looked at the gardens, etc. while my wife went inside. They have a lot of stairs and things you can climb in, but my wife wasn’t interested in climbing to the top of the bell towers, pagodas, drum towers, etc. The next day we visited the Terra Cotta Warriors site . This facility was about 90% accessible and very exciting to visit. They have an entrance where they drive you in large carts up to the buildings surrounding the tombs. I had to transfer into one of the seats and they literally hung my wheelchair on the back of the cart. The three tombs all had ramps to get into them, but in tomb 1 you could only get into the front area. The other tombs were completely accessible. In Xian, we stayed at the Hilton Xi’an . Chengdu We next flew from Xian to Chengdu . Again, we had issues at the airport. The airport was very accessible, but they just don’t know how to handle people in wheelchairs. We were told that I would not be able to take my chair through security. We explained that I needed to stay in my chair until I got on the plane. We argued until we turned blue in the face, but we realized we weren’t going to be able to get on this plane if I didn’t check my chair at the check-in desk. We waited until the last possible minute and then checked it, and they wheeled me through the terminal in their chair. Again, there was no aisle chair, so I was dragged to a seat by a couple of flight attendants. We arrived in Chengdu, and I was relieved that my chair made it and was still in one piece. We had some more issues in Chengdu with our hotel, Hotel Sofitel . This was the one city where we were staying in a Chinese hotel. We were brought to a beautiful room. It had a bedroom, a living room, an office, and two bathrooms. Unfortunately, neither of them was accessible for me to be able to shower or bathe. We were shown another room that they called accessible. (It had one handle in the shower.) It was a much smaller room, but I could fit in and get to a bed. I also decided that I could manage to get into this shower if they had a shower chair. They did not, but they said they could find something for me. They brought me a metal stool that I made work. It wasn’t ideal, but it was doable. The next morning we were off to see the Pandas! While this is a relatively hilly area, it was accessible. I will say I was worn out from pushing up hills, but there were no stairs at the Panda Preserve . The only negative to wheelchair access was they had environmentally friendly landscape pavers. They have gaps for drainage, so it made it a little difficult for my front casters. All in all the pandas made my day! My favorite pastime in Chengdu is to sit at the tea houses, drink tea, and talk, so that is what we did. Later, we visited some more temples and a market. There were stairs and large thresholds, but you could see what Chengdu was all about. Shanghai Then we flew from Chengdu to Shanghai . Again, we had issues at the airport. Although the airports were very modern and had jetways, a lot of the planes were loaded on the tarmac. I was able to take my chair through security this time, but we ended up at a gate on the ground floor. As we watched other flights leave from this gate, they were going by bus to their planes. We just kept smiling and waiting for them to call our destination. The gate attendants got us first to go to the bus. There was a fold-out ramp on the bus. When folded out, it was pretty much a 1-to-1 incline. There was no way I could get up on my own, but the driver helped me get my chair onto the bus. Everyone else got on the bus and filtered around me. We were the last to get off the bus, and we waited for everyone to board the plane up the stairs. I looked around and there was no aisle chair or anything. We had one female escort and I saw one of the baggage handlers give her a thumbs-up. The baggage handler came over to us and then patted himself on the back. I laughed at him and shook my head no. Let me just say I am 6’1” tall and about 200 lbs. He was maybe 5’7” in heels and probably 160 lbs. I transferred to the stairs of the plane and was going to push my way up on my rear. He again patted himself on the back and bent down. I reluctantly put my arms around him. He picked me up and carried me up the stairs on his back. This was ok until we got on the plane. It was too narrow for him to hold my legs, so he had to let go and drag me to my seat. Again, we made it onto another plane and wondered what awaited us in Shanghai. Once everyone was off the plane in Shanghai, I was amazed that they produced an aisle chair to get me off the plane. They also had a lift truck for handicapped people that was at the plane door with my chair inside. That truck took me to the terminal without having to get on the other bus. Shanghai was more modern than the other cities we had been to in China. We visited museums, the Bund, a silk factory, and some markets. All were relatively accessible. We stayed at the Westin Hotel , which was also extremely satisfying. We were supposed to go up into one of the highest buildings, but our guide said there was no way to get a wheelchair to the top. We decided not to go. Based on how modern Shanghai is, I’d be willing to bet there was an elevator that she did not know about. Hong Kong We then flew from Shanghai to Hong Kong . I was looking forward to the lift truck taking me to the plane; however, there was a hurricane off the coast that had made it extremely windy. They told me in the terminal that they were not going to be able to use the lift. So I boarded a bus to the plane (this one did not have the flip ramp). People on the bus helped to lift me onto the bus. When we got to the plane there was a couple of baggage personnel to help me on the plane. I showed them how to roll my chair up the stairs backward. This was a much better alternative to being carried up on someone’s back. They had an aisle chair to get me to my seat. When we got to Hong Kong we went to check in at the Renaissance by Marriott . We asked for a handicap-accessible room and they kept asking if we only wanted 1 bed. When we got to the room it was accessible, but the bed was bigger than a twin but smaller than a double. The room was very small and very dark. We went back down and asked if they had one with 2 beds. They did not. We then asked for a regular room to see if we could make it work. We were shown a gorgeous room with a California king bed. I looked at the shower and thought I could make it work. I didn’t tell them that it might require me to take off some parts of the door, but they provided a shower chair, and I made it work. We visited the Peak, the Aberdeen, and several markets. Most things were accessible in Hong Kong. We returned home from Hong Kong through Tokyo with no major problems. Although there were several obstacles to overcome as I pointed out, this was a fantastic trip and doable. You just have to keep an open mind and laugh when things go wrong. My wife and I are already talking about our next trip. ADDITIONAL NOTES Food: We had lunch included in our tours and breakfast was usually included at the hotels. We were served very large portions. I would say it was very much like the Chinese you get in the US, but we did not order anything crazy. My wife is very picky, so we stuck with safe choices. We would say the meals were very oily and weighed heavy on the stomach. Even some of our guides said they couldn’t eat the things we were eating every day. Our tour guides supplied bottled water, and the hotels all had bottled water. It was not a difficult thing to find. Manual vs. Power Wheelchair: From what I saw, a powerchair would not be able to go to most of the sites that I saw. I also don’t know that the airports would know how to handle one inside China. The manual chair was iffy but doable. I saw one other wheelchair while I was in mainland China and that was an elderly person being pushed by a much younger person. I would be willing to bet they could walk. It was a unique site in mainland China. Several times people would come up on the sidewalk and just try to push me because they didn’t think I should be doing it myself.

title: Most Wheelchair Accessible India Temples
text: India is a land of diverse spiritual traditions and is home to some of the most beautiful and ancient temples in the world. While many of these temples were constructed centuries ago without accessibility in mind, there are several that have made significant strides toward becoming wheelchair accessible. This guide highlights some of the most accessible temples in India, detailing pathway makeup, toilet facilities, amenities, barriers, and nearby accommodations. 1. Akshardham Temple, Delhi Akshardham Temple , located in New Delhi, is one of the most modern and accessible temples in India. Known for its stunning architecture and spiritual significance, it offers a serene and enriching experience for visitors. The temple complex has well-paved, wide pathways that are easy to navigate in a wheelchair. Ramps are available at key points throughout the temple, ensuring seamless access to various sections. Accessible restrooms are available at multiple locations within the temple complex, with clearly marked signs. The restrooms are equipped with grab bars and ample space for maneuvering. Wheelchair rentals are available on-site, though it’s recommended to bring your own if possible for comfort. There are accessible seating areas for viewing the temple’s water shows and other events. The temple has an informative exhibition hall, all of which are wheelchair accessible. The main barriers might be the large crowds, especially during weekends and holidays. Visiting during weekdays or off-peak hours is advisable. Nearby Places to Stay: The LaLiT New Delhi: A luxury hotel offering accessible rooms with roll-in showers and all necessary amenities. Vivanta New Delhi, Dwarka: This hotel also provides accessible rooms and services, located within a reasonable distance from the temple. 2. Golden Temple, Amritsar The Golden Temple, also known as Harmandir Sahib , is the holiest shrine in Sikhism. Located in Amritsar, Punjab, it is a beacon of spirituality and is welcoming to visitors of all faiths. The temple complex features smooth, flat marble pathways that are wheelchair-friendly. Ramps are provided for accessing the main prayer hall and the sacred pond (Amrit Sarovar). Accessible toilets are available, with facilities that cater to wheelchair users. The cleanliness of the restrooms is well-maintained by the temple’s management. Free wheelchair services are available at the entrance. The temple’s langar (community kitchen) is accessible and provides free meals to all visitors, with accessible seating options. Drinking water stations and first-aid services are also available. The temple can get crowded, particularly during religious events. It’s advisable to visit during off-peak times. Some areas around the temple may have slight inclines but are generally manageable with assistance. Nearby Places to Stay: Hyatt Regency Amritsar: Offers accessible rooms and is located close to the temple. Ramada Amritsar: Another good option, with accessible facilities and proximity to the Golden Temple. 3. Lotus Temple, Delhi The Lotus Temple , known for its unique lotus-shaped architecture, is a Baháʼí House of Worship in Delhi. It is an architectural marvel and a place of quiet reflection. The temple complex has well-paved, wide pathways with gentle slopes, ideal for wheelchair access. The approach to the temple includes long ramps and smooth surfaces. Accessible restrooms are available within the temple premises. The restrooms are equipped with handrails and are well-maintained. The temple provides a serene environment with accessible seating areas for meditation. The information center and exhibition areas are fully accessible. Drinking water stations are available, and the temple staff are generally very helpful. There are no significant barriers within the temple complex, though the sheer size of the area may require some stamina to cover in one go. Nearby Places to Stay: Eros Hotel New Delhi, Nehru Place: Offers accessible rooms and is close to the temple. The Suryaa New Delhi: Another good option with accessibility features, located a short drive from the Lotus Temple. 4. Iskcon Temple, Bangalore The ISKCON Temple in Bangalore is one of the largest ISKCON temples in the world and is dedicated to Lord Krishna. The temple is modern and has been designed with accessibility in mind. The temple complex has ramps and elevators to facilitate access to the different levels. Pathways are smooth and well-paved, making navigation easy for wheelchair users. Accessible toilets are available within the temple complex, complete with grab bars and spacious interiors. These facilities are regularly cleaned and well-maintained. The temple offers free wheelchair services at the entrance. Accessible seating areas are available for observing temple rituals and ceremonies. The on-site vegetarian restaurant, serving prasadam, is also wheelchair accessible. The main barrier could be the occasional steep ramps, though they are manageable with some assistance. Nearby Places to Stay: Taj Yeshwantpur, Bengaluru: A luxury hotel offering accessible rooms and close proximity to the temple. Shangri-La Bengaluru: Another excellent option with comprehensive accessibility features. 5. Meenakshi Temple, Madurai The Meenakshi Temple in Madurai is a historic and cultural landmark in South India, known for its intricate architecture and spiritual significance. The temple complex features broad, stone-paved pathways that are mostly smooth but can have slight variations in level. Ramps have been installed at key locations to improve access. Accessible toilets are available within the temple premises, although they may not be as modern as those in newer temples. These restrooms are functional and provide the basic amenities needed for wheelchair users. The temple offers wheelchair rental services, although it’s advisable to bring your own for comfort. Accessible seating is available in some parts of the temple, particularly in areas used for religious ceremonies. The temple’s museum is also accessible, offering a rich insight into the temple’s history. The temple’s ancient structure means there are some areas with steps and uneven surfaces that might require assistance. The temple can be very crowded, especially during festivals, which could pose challenges for movement. Nearby Places to Stay: Heritage Madurai: A luxury hotel offering accessible rooms with features like roll-in showers. The Gateway Hotel Pasumalai Madurai: Offers accessible accommodations with a focus on comfort and convenience.

title: Pilgrimage Sites + Wheelchair Travel
text: These pilgrimage sites offer a blend of spiritual significance and accessibility, allowing wheelchair users to experience the profound and sacred environments without compromising on comfort or safety. Each site has made efforts to include ramps, smooth pathways, accessible restrooms, and other facilities to accommodate visitors with mobility challenges. However, it’s important to plan ahead, especially during peak pilgrimage times when crowds can make navigation more challenging. For the best experience, it’s recommended to contact local authorities or travel services to ensure all necessary accommodations are available. 1. Lourdes, France Lourdes is one of the most important pilgrimage sites for Catholics, known for the Marian apparitions reported by Saint Bernadette Soubirous in 1858. Millions of pilgrims visit each year, many seeking healing from the waters of the Lourdes Grotto. Lourdes is one of the most accessible pilgrimage sites in the world, specifically catering to visitors with disabilities. When visiting, find smooth, wide pathways throughout the sanctuary. There are also ramps and elevators for access to different levels of the basilica and other buildings, accessible restrooms, dedicated seating areas for wheelchair users during mass and other ceremonies, and medical facilities. Large crowds during peak pilgrimage seasons can make navigation more challenging, but the site is generally well-equipped to handle these situations. 2. Vatican City (St. Peter’s Basilica), Vatican City As the spiritual and administrative center of the Roman Catholic Church, Vatican City is a pilgrimage destination for Catholics worldwide. St. Peter’s Basilica , built over the tomb of Saint Peter, is a symbol of faith and a masterpiece of Renaissance architecture. St. Peter’s Basilica and the Vatican Museums are highly accessible to wheelchair users, with modern amenities integrated into this historic site including ramps and elevators throughout St. Peter’s Basilica and the Vatican Museums, priority access lines for visitors with disabilities, and accessible restrooms. Wheelchairs are available for rent at the entrance. Some areas have cobblestone pathways that can be slightly bumpy but are generally manageable with assistance. 3. Fatima, Portugal The Sanctuary of Our Lady of Fátima is one of the most significant Catholic pilgrimage sites, commemorating the apparitions of the Virgin Mary to three shepherd children in 1917. Pilgrims come here to pray for peace and healing. The sanctuary is highly accessible, making it a welcoming destination for pilgrims with mobility impairments including wide, smooth paths throughout the sanctuary, ramps and elevators in key areas, accessible restrooms, and wheelchairs available for use on-site. The site is generally flat and easy to navigate, though large crowds during major events could create some challenges. 4. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib), Amritsar, India The Golden Temple, or Harmandir Sahib , is the holiest site in Sikhism. It is a symbol of equality and humility, welcoming people of all faiths to its sacred precincts. The Golden Temple is one of the most accessible religious sites in India, with extensive efforts made to ensure that all visitors, including those in wheelchairs, can fully participate in the spiritual experience. Ramps and smooth pathways throughout the temple complex. Accessible restrooms are also available. There are accessible entrances to the main prayer halls. The community kitchen (langar) is accessible, offering free meals to all. The large crowds, particularly during festivals, can make navigation slower and more challenging, but the site is otherwise very accessible. 5. The Wailing Wall (Western Wall), Jerusalem, Israel The Western Wall is the last remaining structure of the Second Temple, making it the holiest site in Judaism. Jews and people of other faiths come to pray and place written prayers into the cracks of the wall. The Western Wall has made considerable efforts to be accessible to visitors with disabilities with ramps leading to the prayer area, allowing wheelchair users to approach the Wall. Special accommodations for individuals with mobility issues during busy religious observances. Accessible restrooms are nearby. The Old City of Jerusalem can be challenging due to its ancient, uneven streets, but the area immediately surrounding the Western Wall is accessible. 6. Santiago de Compostela, Spain Santiago de Compostela is the culmination of the Camino de Santiago, a major Christian pilgrimage route since the Middle Ages. It is believed to be the final resting place of Saint James the Apostle. The Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela has taken steps to ensure accessibility for pilgrims with disabilities, like ramps and accessible entrances to the cathedral. Wheelchairs available for use within the cathedral. Accessible accommodations can be found along parts of the Camino de Santiago route. The ancient cobblestone streets in Santiago can be bumpy, and some parts of the Camino de Santiago trail are not accessible, so careful planning is needed. 7. Shrine of Imam Hussain, Karbala, Iraq The Shrine of Imam Hussain is a sacred site for Shia Muslims, marking the burial place of Imam Hussain, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was martyred at the Battle of Karbala. The shrine has accessible features for visitors with disabilities such as ramps and smooth pathways within the shrine complex as well as accessible restrooms. Assistance services available during large gatherings, such as Arbaeen. Extremely large crowds during religious events can make accessibility difficult, though the site itself is equipped with accessible features. 8. Sarnath, India Sarnath is one of the four main pilgrimage sites for Buddhists, as it is the place where Buddha gave his first sermon after attaining enlightenment. Sarnath’s main temple and archaeological sites have several accessible features, like ramps and accessible paths at key locations, including the main temple. There are also accessible restrooms. Some areas of the archaeological site may have uneven terrain, though the main temple area is more accessible. 9. Rameswaram, India Rameswaram is a major pilgrimage site in Hinduism, especially for followers of Shaivism. The Ramanathaswamy Temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlinga temples dedicated to Shiva. The temple has made efforts to improve accessibility, although challenges remain. Some ramps and accessible paths are in parts of the temple complex along with accessible restrooms. The temple has many steps and some uneven paths that may require assistance to navigate. The overall infrastructure is improving, but challenges still exist. 10. The Temple of the Tooth, Kandy, Sri Lanka The Temple of the Tooth is a significant Buddhist site, believed to house the relic of the tooth of Buddha. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a place of pilgrimage for Buddhists from around the world. The temple is relatively accessible, with efforts made to accommodate visitors with disabilities, like ramps and accessible pathways within the temple complex as well as accessible restrooms. Some areas of the temple complex may have steps or crowded conditions that could pose difficulties.

title: India Public Bathrooms + Wheelchair Travel
text: Traveling through India offers an incredible array of experiences, from bustling cities and historical monuments to tranquil rural landscapes. However, for wheelchair users, finding accessible public bathrooms can be a challenge. While the country is making strides toward improved accessibility, there is still a long way to go. This guide provides an overview of wheelchair-accessible public bathrooms in India, including tips on where to find them, what to expect, and how to plan your trip. India is a diverse country with a mix of modern and traditional infrastructure. While newer buildings and public spaces are increasingly designed with accessibility in mind, many older facilities remain challenging for wheelchair users. The Indian government has initiated the “ Accessible India Campaign” (Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan ) to promote accessibility, but progress varies across regions. Types of Accessible Public Bathrooms Accessible public bathrooms in India generally fall into two categories: Government-Provided Facilities : These are often found at airports, railway stations, bus terminals, and some tourist sites. They are designed to meet basic accessibility standards, including ramps, wider doorways, and grab bars. Private Establishments : Malls, hotels, large restaurants, and modern office buildings often provide accessible bathrooms. These are typically more reliable in terms of cleanliness and modern amenities. Key Locations for Accessible Bathrooms Airports : Airports in India are generally well-equipped with accessible facilities, including bathrooms. Major international airports like Indira Gandhi International Airport (Delhi), Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (Mumbai), and Kempegowda International Airport (Bangalore) all have accessible restrooms. Visitors can expect to find wide doorways, grab bars, ample space for maneuvering, and emergency call buttons are standard features. Cleanliness is generally well-maintained, and staff are often available to assist. Railway Stations : Major railway stations, especially in metropolitan areas, are increasingly being equipped with accessible restrooms. However, availability and quality can vary significantly. Accessible bathrooms are usually located near the entrance or waiting areas. These bathrooms typically have ramps, grab bars, and enough space for a wheelchair, though cleanliness can sometimes be an issue. Shopping Malls : Large shopping malls in cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Bangalore, and Chennai usually have accessible bathrooms. These are generally modern, clean, and well-maintained. Malls often provide the most reliable accessible facilities, with clean restrooms, grab bars, and spacious interiors. They are usually located near food courts or at designated restroom areas on each floor. Hotels and Restaurants : High-end hotels and chain restaurants in urban areas are more likely to have accessible bathrooms. Mid-range and budget accommodations may vary in terms of accessibility. Accessible bathrooms in hotels are typically part of the accessible guest rooms, while in restaurants, they are often located on the ground floor. Expect modern amenities like grab bars, roll-in showers (in hotels), and space for maneuvering. Tourist Attractions : Accessible restrooms are available at some popular tourist destinations, especially those that have seen recent renovations. However, many historical sites, particularly those located in older buildings or remote areas, may lack accessible facilities. Where available, these bathrooms are typically basic but functional, with ramps, grab bars, and enough space for a wheelchair. Cleanliness and maintenance can vary widely. Challenges and Tips for Visitors Challenges Inconsistent Availability : While accessibility is improving, there are still many places, particularly in rural areas and smaller towns, where accessible public bathrooms are scarce. Maintenance Issues : Even when accessible bathrooms are available, they may not always be well-maintained. Lack of regular cleaning and inadequate supplies can be common problems. Older Buildings : Many of India’s historic sites and older buildings were not designed with accessibility in mind, making it difficult to find suitable facilities. Tips Plan Ahead : Before visiting a location, check online resources or call ahead to confirm the availability of accessible restrooms. Apps like “Google Maps” often include information on restroom accessibility. Use Accessible Apps : Apps such as “Wheelmap” allow users to find and review wheelchair-accessible places, including bathrooms. These can be helpful in planning your day or finding nearby facilities. Leverage Hotel Facilities : If you’re staying in a hotel, make use of the accessible facilities there before heading out. This can minimize the need to rely on public restrooms. Malls and Large Stores : In urban areas, shopping malls, large supermarkets, and department stores are often your best bet for clean and accessible restrooms. Ask for Help : Don’t hesitate to ask locals or staff members at attractions for information on the nearest accessible restroom. In many cases, they’ll be able to guide you to suitable facilities. Improving Accessibility in India India’s journey towards comprehensive accessibility is ongoing. Efforts such as the Accessible India Campaign and increasing awareness among private businesses are helping to improve the situation. However, for now, accessible facilities remain concentrated in urban areas and at major tourist attractions. Traveling in India as a wheelchair user requires careful planning and patience, but with the right preparation, it is possible to enjoy a comfortable and enriching experience. By focusing on well-maintained, accessible facilities and planning your route accordingly, you can make the most of your visit to this diverse and culturally rich country.
